pathwayLabel: Certification by Endorsement — 10-Year Licensure History (Option C)
examName: None required under Option C — a passed licensing exam is only required if applying under Option A (NASCLA route) instead
steps: California is not Florida's one confirmed reciprocal-agreement state (Louisiana) — the $350 CILB 32 reciprocity form and fee do not apply to a California license.

Instead, apply via DBPR CILB 10, Certification by Endorsement (Section 489.115(3), Florida Statutes). The most broadly applicable route for a California contractor is Option C: hold a valid, current out-of-state license for at least 10 years, active now or within the last 2 years.

If your California license was earned via the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor exam instead, Option A may apply: pass Florida's Business and Finance exam and attest to passing an exam on the Florida Building Code — this route does not require 10 years of licensure.
Complete a board-approved 2-hour Florida Building Code course covering wind mitigation techniques (required for Certified General/Building/Residential/Roofing Contractor categories).
Submit electronic fingerprints, a FICO-derived credit report, and proof of satisfaction of any liens, judgments, or bankruptcy.
Pay the $354 Endorsement application fee to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
Await processing — DBPR does not publish a guaranteed timeline for this form; budget for several weeks to a few months.
notes: Fee and process confirmed directly from DBPR CILB 10 (Application for Certification by Endorsement, Section 489.115(3), F.S.): $354 fee, three applicant options (A: passed a substantially equivalent exam, primarily used for NASCLA; B: license issued under substantially equivalent criteria, discretionary and described by DBPR's own form as 'very stringent and rarely approved'; C: 10+ years continuously active out-of-state license). California is not a reciprocal-agreement state (confirmed from the separate CILB 32 reciprocity form, which lists only Louisiana), so the $350 reciprocity fee and process do not apply here — this is a distinct, more broadly available pathway. UNRESOLVED CONFLICT between two official DBPR documents, flagged rather than silently resolved: CILB 10's own text states 'there are currently no reciprocal agreements in place to recognize valid licenses in other states or territories' under its Option D, while the separate CILB 32 form (effective July 2024) explicitly lists one active reciprocal state (Louisiana). These appear to be two legally distinct mechanisms under the same statute (endorsement vs. reciprocity), but the CILB 10 form's own wording is stale or contradictory on this point — treat Option D of CILB 10 as unreliable and use the CILB 32 form as authoritative for reciprocity specifically. Source note: DBPR's own domain (myfloridalicense.com) blocks automated fetches of this document (403); the content was retrieved from flrules.org, the Florida Administrative Register — the same document, incorporated by reference under F.A.C. rule, hosted on Florida's official rulemaking site rather than DBPR's own. CORRECTION (2026-09-20): this record originally stated CILB 32's reciprocal-state list as 'Louisiana, Mississippi, and North Carolina.' That was wrong. Re-verified by running antiword directly on the raw CILB 32 .doc binary (bypassing both flrules.org's Cloudflare bot-challenge, which blocks plain curl, and any AI-summarization step) — a full-text search of the complete extracted document found 'Louisiana' three times, in the three license-category checkboxes, and zero occurrences of 'Mississippi' or 'North Carolina' anywhere. The form's instructions do reference an external hyperlink ('a list of states which have entered into a reciprocity agreement... can be found by visiting this link') whose destination this extraction can't follow, so a broader, separately-maintained list is conceivable — but the form's own selectable categories, which is what actually matters for an applicant, name only Louisiana. This record's conclusion (California doesn't qualify for reciprocity either way) is unaffected by the correction.
officialSourceName: Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation, Construction Industry Licensing Board (DBPR CILB)
